sections.title: *Pidyon Ha'ben* Proof: Fixed Value, or the Kohen's Own Valuation?
sections.gist: This continues Rav Yosef's attempt to prove that *shaveh kesef* must have a set value. The reply, in line with Rabba, reads the *pidyon ha'ben* baraita as a kohen who chose to value the item at five *sela*, as Rav Kahana did, and Rav Ashi limits this to a great man.

bullets.text: The reply to Rav Yosef, in line with Rabba: in the *pidyon ha'ben* baraita the calf or cloak is actually worth less than five *sela* in both clauses. The second clause works because the kohen accepted it as worth five *sela* to himself.
Precedent: Rav Kahana took a cloth from the house of a man redeeming his firstborn and said, "For me, this cloth is worth five *sela*."
Rav Ashi: this works only for someone like Rav Kahana, a great man who needs a cloth for his head. For everyone else it does not.
Proof that such a man will pay above value: Mar bar Rav Ashi bought a cloth from Rabba's mother, from Kovei, for thirteen dinars, though it was worth ten.

The two readings expose the core disagreement. For Rav Yosef, *shaveh kesef* stands in for money, so it must share money's defining trait, a fixed value. For Rabba, it is an object of value in its own right, so a credible personal valuation is enough.
The limit is about credibility. An ordinary person's claim that a trifle is worth five *sela* to him is disregarded, since no one in his position would pay that much.
Tosafot suggests Rav Kahana may not have been a kohen himself but married to a kohen's daughter. That would mean a kohen's daughter can also receive the redemption payment.

The halakha follows Rabba: silk needs no appraisal. Rabbeinu Tam (Tosafot) explains that silk's value is roughly known. Precious stones and pearls vary so widely that she cannot rely on a claimed value, so they do need appraisal.

Hence the custom Tosafot records of betrothing with a ring that has no stone. It is also why, at the *chuppah*, the witnesses confirm only that the ring is worth at least a *perutah*: no specific value is represented.

sections.title: A Hundred Promised, One Dinar Given: Condition or Full Payment?
sections.gist: R. Elazar treats a hundred promised with one dinar handed over as a betrothal *al menat*. A baraita about counting out a hundred challenges him, which leads to three readings: "this hundred", the latter clause explaining the first, and Rav Ashi's point that counting is different. The Gemara then turns to the copper and flawed dinars.

chart.caption: The hundred-dinar cases and their rulings
rows: Unspecified hundred promised, one dinar given (R. Elazar)
Betrothed at once; he completes the rest
The hundred is a condition (*al menat*), which takes effect "from now"
Counting out a hundred; one side retracts before the last dinar
Not betrothed
The case is "this hundred", so the whole sum is the money; or (Rav Ashi) counting shows she expects all of it
"This hundred", found one dinar short
Not betrothed
It is not the sum he named
"This hundred", one copper dinar among them
Not betrothed
Given at night or mixed in, so she never knowingly accepted it
"This hundred", one flawed dinar that can be spent with difficulty
Betrothed; he exchanges it
It still passes as money (Rav Pappa)

children.title: R. Elazar: One Dinar Now, the Hundred *Al Menat*
children.gist: Promising a hundred and handing over one dinar betroths at once: the dinar is the money, and the hundred becomes a condition that works "from now".

bullets.text: R. Elazar: he said "Be betrothed to me with a hundred dinars" and gave her one. She is betrothed immediately, and he must complete the payment.
Reason: saying a hundred but giving one is like saying "on condition that I give you a hundred". The one dinar betroths now, and the remaining ninety-nine are owed.
This follows Rav Huna in the name of Rav: whoever says *al menat* is as if he said "from now" (*ke'omer me'akhshav dami*), so it takes effect immediately.
The act of handing over a single dinar clarifies his intent: it marks the dinar as the *kesef kiddushin* and turns the hundred into a condition.

children.title: Counting Out a Hundred: "This Hundred", Explanation, or Counting Is Different
children.gist: A baraita lets either side retract until the last dinar is counted. The Gemara reads it as "this hundred" and defends that reading against the latter clause, and Rav Ashi offers that counting itself shows she expects the whole sum.

children.title: The Objection and the "This Hundred" Answer
children.gist: The counting baraita seems to contradict R. Elazar. The Gemara answers that it speaks of "this hundred", but the latter clause's own "this hundred" suggests the first clause is unspecified.

bullets.text: Objection (Tosefta 2:10): "Be betrothed with a hundred dinars", and while he was counting one of them retracted. Either may do so even at the last dinar, so the betrothal waits for the full hundred.
Answer: the case is "with this hundred dinars", where the whole hundred is the betrothal money.
Challenge: the latter clause says "this hundred" explicitly, which implies the first clause is an unspecified hundred.
The latter clause: "this hundred" found a dinar short, or with a copper dinar, means not betrothed. With a flawed dinar she is betrothed, and he must exchange it.

children.title: Both Clauses "This Hundred": The Latter Clause Explains the First
children.gist: Both clauses can be read as "this hundred", with the latter clause explaining the first. A supporting argument is offered and shown to be inconclusive.

bullets.text: Reply: both clauses speak of "this hundred". The latter clause explains the first: "Either may retract until the last dinar. How so? When he said: with this hundred."
Support: if the first clause were an unspecified hundred and still no betrothal, it would go without saying for "this hundred", and the latter clause would be superfluous.
The support is rejected. The latter clause could be there to show that the first clause is an unspecified hundred, so that one would not limit it to "this hundred".
The proof falls away, but the reading of the first clause as "this hundred" remains available.

children.title: Rav Ashi: Counting Is Different
children.gist: No need for "this hundred": when he counts coin by coin, both expect the whole hundred, so either may retract until he finishes.

bullets.text: Rav Ashi: counting is different. She has the whole hundred in mind and won't settle for part of it.
His ongoing counting shows both sides expect the full sum, so either may retract until he finishes. R. Elazar's case, where he hands over one dinar and stops, stands.

children.title: Copper Dinar vs. Flawed Dinar: Unseen, or Spendable with Difficulty
children.gist: Why a copper dinar voids the betrothal though she took it, and what a flawed dinar is: one that can be spent, with difficulty.

bullets.text: Copper dinar: if she knew it was copper, she accepted it as it was. The answer: he gave it at night, or it was mixed in among the others and she didn't notice.
Flawed dinar: if it can't be spent at all, it is just like copper. Rav Pappa: it can be spent with difficulty.
A flawed dinar is still genuine currency. She received in substance what was promised, so the betrothal holds and he replaces the coin. A copper coin is simply not what he promised.

returns_to.note: Analyzes the cases in the latter clause of the counting baraita

sections.title: *Mashkon*: "No Hundred Here, No *Mashkon* Here"
sections.gist: Rav Nachman rules that his own *mashkon* for a promised hundred does not betroth. A baraita allowing betrothal with a *mashkon* is limited to another's *mashkon*, which a creditor owns (R. Yitzchak), and R. Ami applies the rule to a sale.

chart.caption: Giving a *mashkon* in place of payment
rows: His own *mashkon* for a promised hundred (Rav Nachman)
Not betrothed
The hundred wasn't given, and the *mashkon* is only security, not a gift
Another person's *mashkon* that he holds (baraita)
Betrothed
A creditor acquires the *mashkon* (R. Yitzchak), so he gives something that is his
A piece of silver as a *mashkon* for a maidservant's price (R. Ami)
Sale not complete
"No *perutot* here, no piece of silver here"

children.title: Rav Nachman's Ruling and Rava's Objection: Whose *Mashkon*?
children.gist: His own *mashkon* in place of a promised hundred does not betroth; the baraita that allows it speaks of a *mashkon* belonging to others.

bullets.text: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman: "Be betrothed with a hundred dinars", and he gave her a *mashkon* for the money instead. She is not betrothed.
"No hundred here, no *mashkon* here": the hundred hasn't been given, and the *mashkon* is only security, not a gift. He has given her nothing.
Rava objects from a baraita: if he betrothed her with a *mashkon*, she is betrothed.
Answer: that baraita means a *mashkon* belonging to others, held by the man, in line with R. Yitzchak.
Like Yehudah's pledge to Tamar, a *mashkon* guarantees a future payment; it is not the payment itself.

children.title: R. Yitzchak: A Creditor Acquires the *Mashkon*
children.gist: Returning a pledge is called "righteousness", so the creditor must own it to some degree; hence he can betroth with it.

bullets.text: R. Yitzchak: Devarim 24:13, "restore him the pledge... and it shall be righteousness to you". If the creditor didn't acquire it, how would returning it be righteousness? So he acquires it to a degree.

Tosafot objects that returning a garment so a poor man can sleep is kind in any case. Tosafot proposes that the verse's "and bless you" would be *ribit devarim* unless the garment is the creditor's own, and that *tzedakah* means giving from one's own.
Tosafot distinguishes a *mashkon* taken when the loan was made from one taken afterward, and infers ownership in both.

Example: Reuven holds Shimon's watch as a *mashkon* and betroths with it, giving something he owns. What she actually gets, when she can't use the watch and may not collect the debt, is left open; perhaps transferring something he owns is enough.

children.title: Rav Huna bar Avin's Sons: A Silver Piece Is Not the Price
children.gist: The same rule in a sale: a piece of silver left as a *mashkon* for the price of a maidservant does not complete the purchase.

bullets.text: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin bought a maidservant for copper *perutot*. They didn't have the money, so they left a piece of silver as a *mashkon*.
Her price rose, and the sellers wanted to cancel. R. Ami: "No *perutot* here, no piece of silver here." There was no acquisition.
Tosafot: no debt existed yet, so what did the *mashkon* secure, and could the sellers force completion? The question is left partly open.

sections.title: Her Response to the Money: Rejection, Agency, or Her Own Property
sections.gist: A run of baraitot on what she does with the money: destroying it, sending it to a father or to so-and-so, with or without agency ("on condition he accepts it for me"), and having it put on a rock or given to a dog. Two cases are left as *teiku*.

sections.continues: Continues with "give it to a poor person", even one she supports, and then a series of cases of offhand replies such as "give, give".

children.title: Thrown into Sea or Fire: Rejection, Not a Test of His Temper
children.gist: Destroying the money is still refusal. The baraita needs to say so because her liability to repay might suggest she took it as betrothal money.

bullets.text: Baraita (Tosefta 2:9): she took the hundred and threw it into the sea, into the fire, or into anything that destroys. She is not betrothed.
The Gemara is surprised: this implies that throwing it back before him would be a betrothal, yet that plainly says "take it, I don't want it".

Answer: the baraita teaches that throwing it before him obviously isn't betrothal. Destroying it is the new point: since she must pay him back, one might think she accepted the money and was testing whether he has an angry temper. She is still not betrothed.
If she rejected him, the money was never hers. The liability that destroying it creates could be misread as a sign that she took it as her own.

children.title: "Give It to My Father / Your Father": Only "On Condition He Accepts It for Me"
children.gist: Sending the money to either father is refusal, unless she adds that he should accept it for her. Each father shows how far one clause reaches.

bullets.text: Baraita (Tosefta 2:9): "Give it to my father" or "to your father": not betrothed. "...On condition that he accepts it for me": betrothed.
"My father" shows how far the first clause reaches: even to her own father, whom she would want to benefit, she is not betrothed.
"Your father" shows how far the second clause reaches: with the condition, even his father can receive it for her.
Without the condition she is mocking him: go waste your money elsewhere. With it, she appoints the recipient as her *shaliach* to accept the *kiddushin*.

children.title: So-and-So as Well: Why Both Cases Are Needed
children.gist: The same rulings for so-and-so, and why neither case could be learned from the other: trust in relatives, and closeness that might suggest a gift.

bullets.text: A parallel baraita: "Give it to so-and-so" is not a betrothal. "On condition that he accepts it for me" is a betrothal. Why state both cases?
Had only the fathers been taught: the condition works there because she relies on relatives to hold the money for her. With so-and-so, one would say it doesn't.

Had only so-and-so been taught: without the condition it fails because she isn't close to him and intends no gift. With a father, one might think she accepted the money and passed it on as a gift, so she would be betrothed.
So both are needed. Without the condition there is no betrothal even to a father, and with it even so-and-so can receive.
Rashi: this differs from "give a hundred to so-and-so and I will be betrothed to you", where she set up the arrangement herself. Here she is mocking him.

children.title: Place It on a Rock: Hers, Not Hers, or Shared (*Teiku*)
children.gist: On her own rock the money is received, and on another's rock it is not. Rav Beivai's question about a rock they both own is left unresolved.

bullets.text: Baraita: "Place them on a rock": not betrothed. If the rock is hers, she is betrothed.
Rav Beivai: what if the rock belongs to both of them? *Teiku*.
Rashi: on her own rock she acquires the money through *kinyan chatzer*.

Tosafot: if it were *kinyan chatzer*, the shared rock would be simple, since partners don't acquire from each other in shared property. The test is rather her confidence that she can retrieve the money, which is unclear on a shared rock.
The Gemara here seems concerned less with a perfect formal *kinyan* than with what counts as her acceptance for *kiddushin*.

children.title: Give It to a Dog: Hers, Not Hers, or One Chasing Her
children.gist: A loaf fed to her own dog betroths, and to another's dog it does not. Rav Mari asks about a dog attacking her.

bullets.text: "Be betrothed with a loaf of bread"; she said "give it to a dog": not betrothed. If the dog is hers, she is betrothed.
Does she acquire the loaf through her dog, an extension of *kinyan chatzer*, or is the betrothal money the *hana'ah* of having her dog fed at his expense? The shiur leaves this open.

children.title: A Dog Chasing Her: Rescue as *Hana'ah* or a Duty He Owes? *Teiku*
children.gist: If throwing the loaf saves her from a dog, is the rescue a benefit that betroths, or something he was obligated to do anyway? The question is left unresolved.

bullets.text: Rav Mari: a dog was chasing her to bite her, and she said "give the loaf to the dog". What is the law?

Perhaps she commits herself through the *hana'ah* of being rescued. Or perhaps she can say: you were obligated to rescue me anyway, under "do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbor" (Vayikra 19:16), so she owes him nothing.
*Teiku*: the question stands.

key_terms.sense: an item of monetary value used as payment
key_terms.definition: Property that is worth money and may be used in place of coins in a transaction that requires payment, such as betrothal or the redemption of a Hebrew slave.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rabba and Rav Yosef dispute whether it must have a set value like money, and the pidyon ha'ben baraita is read to fit each view.

key_terms.definition: The obligation of a father to redeem his firstborn son by giving a kohen five sela, or goods worth that amount.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Whether a calf or cloak redeems when the kohen accepts it as worth five sela to himself, as Rav Kahana did with a cloth.

key_terms.sense: a condition that takes effect immediately
key_terms.definition: A stipulation phrased "on condition that". In the view of Rav Huna in Rav's name it is as if he said "from now": the act takes effect at once, and is void if the condition is not fulfilled.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Elazar treats "betrothed with a hundred", with only one dinar given, as betrothal al menat, so the dinar betroths now and the rest is owed.

key_terms.definition: An item a debtor gives or a creditor takes as security for a loan or payment, to be returned when the debt is paid.
key_terms.on_this_daf: His own mashkon in place of promised money does not betroth, but a mashkon belonging to others that he holds does, since a creditor acquires it (R. Yitzchak).

key_terms.sense: an agent acting on another's behalf
key_terms.definition: A person appointed to perform a legal act for someone else, whose act counts as the principal's own.
key_terms.on_this_daf: "On condition that he accepts it for me" makes her father, his father or so-and-so her agent to receive the kiddushin money.

key_terms.definition: The principle that a person's property, such as a courtyard or field, can acquire objects placed in it on the owner's behalf.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rashi explains that money placed on her own rock betroths through kinyan chatzer; Tosafot argues the shared-rock question points to her confidence of retrieval instead.

key_terms.sense: a benefit serving as the betrothal payment
key_terms.definition: A benefit of monetary value given to a woman, which can serve as the payment of kiddushin in place of an object or money handed to her.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Mari asks whether being rescued from a dog is a benefit that betroths, or a duty the man owed her anyway.

judgment_calls: The first section (8a.10–8a.11) is a single section without children. Rabba's reading, Rav Kahana's precedent and Rav Ashi's limit are short steps in one reply. The shiur's material on the ruling for silk, Rabbeinu Tam's distinction for precious stones and the plain-ring custom has no line of its own in the text, so it sits in that section as shiur bullets.

R. Elazar's ruling, the counting baraita and the copper and flawed dinars are grouped under one parent, since the baraita is brought as an objection to R. Elazar. They could also be three top-level sections.

The copper and flawed dinar analysis could nest under the "this hundred" answer (s5), where those cases are quoted. It is kept as a sibling with a returns_to link, because it comes after the whole exchange about the two clauses and Rav Ashi.
Rav Ashi's counting distinction is placed as the third reading within the counting-baraita section rather than as its own top-level section, since it is an alternative answer to the same objection.

The mashkon discussion is its own top-level section, although it opens with "a hundred dinars" like R. Elazar's case, because its question (a pledge as payment) is new. Rav Huna bar Avin's sons, a sale, is kept under it because R. Ami applies the same formula.
The dog-chasing question is a flagged child of the dog case, not a sibling, because it varies that same baraita.
The "so-and-so" baraita is a separate section with a returns_to link to the fathers' case, not merged into it, because the Gemara gives it its own explanation of why both are needed.
coverage_notes: Lines 8a.1–8a.9 fall outside this outline's scope: Rav Yosef's set-value principle, the Hebrew-slave baraita, the reading of it as symbolic exchange (chalipin) with Rav Nachman's objection, and Rav Yosef's pidyon ha'ben proof. The essay's sections on them are used only as context for s1.

The essay says the Gemara concludes "vehilchesa shiraim lo tzrichi shuma". No such line appears in the provided text for this range, so the ruling and Tosafot's discussion of it are presented as shiur material.
The essay attributes the "only a great man" limitation to Mar bar Rav Ashi; the text has Rav Ashi, with Mar bar Rav Ashi's purchase as the supporting incident. Followed the text.
The essay says Rav Kahana was possibly not a kohen (Tosafot). This is kept as the shiur's point; the outline does not assert either way in Gemara bullets.
The segmentation and essay call him "Rav Yitzchak"; the text has R. Yitzchak. Followed the text.
The essay has "Rav Ami"; the text has R. Ami. It also says the sons were paying with "priti" (cash), while the text specifies copper perutot. Followed the text.
The essay has "Rav Bibi"; the text has Rav Beivai. Followed the text.

The essay's account of the reisha/seifa exchange is muddled: it says the Gemara "settles on the simpler reading: the seifa introduces a genuine chiddush". The outline follows the text's order: the "this hundred" answer, the inference from the latter clause, both clauses read as "this hundred", the supporting argument, and its rejection.

The essay does not discuss Rav Ashi's "counting is different" (8a.20); that section is outlined from the text and flagged. The essay also skips the question of how she took a copper dinar (at night, or mixed in); this is outlined from the text within s8.

The essay says the Gemara leaves open whether a dog betroths through acquisition or through the benefit of feeding it. The text does not raise that question; it is kept as shiur analysis. The text's own question, Rav Mari's dog chasing her (teiku), is not in the shiur and is outlined from the text and flagged.
The shiur's Tosafot material on mashkon (ribit devarim, tzedakah from one's own, pre-debt pledges) is kept as shiur bullets.
Line 8b.14 ("give it to a poor person") and 8b.15 onward fall outside this outline's scope.
